prediction.likelyOutcome: The court will almost certainly award the landlord a rent deficiency (accrued rent net of reletting income, plus late fees and prejudgment interest) closer to Kolaj's ~$96,000 computation than to the landlord's $538,000 acceleration theory, because the lease's plain terms tie acceleration to a landlord's decision NOT to relet, and the landlord did relet. The $300,000 kitchen claim is likely to fail or be awarded only nominally given the total absence of value/benefit proof at trial, while a substantial (if somewhat trimmed) attorney's fee award is likely given undisputed prevailing-party status under both the lease and Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 38.001.

outcome.description: After the bench trial the trial court rendered judgment for the landlord of $96,072.49 (unpaid rent through trial net of replacement-tenant rent, late fees, and prejudgment interest) — the figure the tenant advocated, roughly one-tenth of the more than $900,000 the landlord sought — plus 18% post-judgment interest, and awarded $0 in attorneys' fees. The court of appeals affirmed the damages award and reversed only the denial of attorneys' fees, remanding for a determination of a reasonable fee under the lease.
outcome.finalNote: Damages affirmed; fee denial reversed and remanded.
